name: Parijata Vaneswarar Temple, Tirukkalar
deity: Shiva as Parijata Vaneswarar (Kalarmulainathar), with the goddess Amudhavalli
tradition: Shaiva — a Paadal Petra Sthalam, sung by Sambandar and Appar
summary: Tirukkalar, near Mannargudi, is where Shiva is said to have danced the Brahma Tandavam for the sage Durvasa, who had carried the heavenly parijata flower to earth to see the lord's dance. Shiva is worshipped here as Parijata Vaneswarar — lord of the parijata grove — also praised as Kalarmulainathar, with the goddess Amudhavalli. A Paadal Petra Sthalam sung by Sambandar and Appar, its tall eastern rajagopuram marks it from afar across the delta.

sections.history: Tirukkalar is an ancient Shaiva village near Mannargudi, revered in the seventh-century Tevaram and counted among the Paadal Petra Sthalams, sung by both Sambandar and Appar. The stone temple belongs to the Chola period with later additions; by tradition the first consecration was performed by the sage Durvasa himself. The place name is explained from the Tamil word for the dance floor, tying the village from the start to the legend of Shiva's dance.
sections.architecture: The temple follows the Dravidian plan, dominated by a tall, five-tiered rajagopuram rising about eighty feet and facing east. The sanctum enshrines the lingam of Parijata Vaneswarar, and the goddess Amudhavalli has her own shrine. The grand eastern tower, visible far across the flat delta country, gives this otherwise village temple the presence of a major shrine.
sections.legends: The defining legend is the dance of Shiva for Durvasa. The sage, hearing of the cosmic dance the lord performed at Chidambaram, longed to witness it; he brought the parijata flower from the world of the gods and planted it here, and Shiva, pleased with his devotion, came down and danced the Brahma Tandavam before him. From the grove of parijata the lord takes his name, Parijata Vaneswarar, and from the dance floor the village and the lord's other name, Kalarmulainathar, are drawn.
sections.festivals: The temple keeps the Shaiva festival calendar — Maha Shivaratri, Pradosham, the Margazhi season and the annual Brahmotsavam — with the dance legend lending special meaning to the festivals of Nataraja and Arudra Darshan. The tall gopuram makes the car festival and processions a landmark event for the surrounding villages.
sections.experience: Approaching Tirukkalar across the delta, the pilgrim sees the great eastern tower long before the village itself. Within, the darshan of Parijata Vaneswarar carries the memory of a dance performed for a single devoted sage, and of a heavenly flower rooted in delta soil — a tender image at the heart of a temple that wears its antiquity lightly.

visit.timings: Typically open from early morning to midday and again from late afternoon into the evening; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected, with shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left at the entrance.
visit.photography: Photography is generally allowed in the outer corridors but not inside the sanctum; ask temple staff before photographing rituals.
visit.gettingThere: Tirukkalar is in Tiruvarur district near Mannargudi, roughly 10-12 km away; Mannargudi is the nearest town and rail head, with local buses and taxis to the village.
